question: Pre-Reading: Work in groups of three and write down at least three health-related problems that people in your area face. Also list what steps people should take to protect themselves from some of these problems. Write these in your notebook in the given format (Health Problems - Problem 1 - Steps for protection).
answer: HEALTH PROBLEMS. Problem 1: Mosquito-borne diseases such as malaria, dengue and chikungunya. Steps for protection: Do not let water collect around the house; clean water tanks, coolers and flower pots regularly; keep buckets, pots and tyres covered so that there is no stagnant water; use mosquito nets and wear clothes that cover the body; apply mosquito repellent; and seek medical help as soon as symptoms appear. Problem 2: Contaminated drinking water causing diarrhoea, cholera and typhoid. Steps for protection: Drink boiled or filtered water, keep drinking water covered, wash hands with soap before eating, and keep the kitchen and toilets clean. Problem 3: Air pollution causing cough, asthma and chest infections. Steps for protection: Keep the house well ventilated, avoid burning garbage or plastic, plant more trees, and wear a mask when the air is dusty or smoky.
explanation: This pre-reading task draws on learners' prior knowledge about common health problems in their locality so that they can connect it with the reading text on diseases caused by mosquitoes.

question: Tick the right answer. The text is about:
answer: c) Diseases caused by mosquitoes
explanation: The whole passage deals with malaria, dengue and chikungunya, all of which are spread by mosquitoes, so option (c) correctly states the central idea.

question: Circle the diseases mentioned in the text: tuberculosis, diphtheria, cholera, yellow fever, jaundice, malaria, tonsillitis, chikungunya, hepatitis, dengue, influenza, cerebral malaria.
answer: The diseases mentioned in the text are: malaria, dengue, chikungunya and cerebral malaria (a severe form of malaria). All the other names listed (tuberculosis, diphtheria, cholera, yellow fever, jaundice, tonsillitis, hepatitis and influenza) do not appear in the passage.
explanation: The reading text discusses only the three mosquito-borne diseases - malaria, dengue and chikungunya - and mentions cerebral malaria as a complication of malaria, so only those four names are to be circled.

question: Read the text. Find the following words and underline them: parasite, transmitted, saliva, clot, chills, constipation, dysfunction, disorientation, transfusion, antibodies, immune, respiratory, stagnant, contagious, nausea, fatal, display, inflammation, intense, pronounced.
answer: All twenty words occur in the text. Their meanings are: parasite - an organism that lives on or inside another organism and feeds on it; transmitted - passed on from one person or thing to another; saliva - the watery liquid produced in the mouth; clot - to change from liquid into a thick, semi-solid mass; chills - a feeling of coldness accompanied by shivering; constipation - difficulty in emptying the bowels; dysfunction - the abnormal or impaired working of an organ; disorientation - confusion about time, place or identity; transfusion - the transfer of blood from one person into another; antibodies - proteins produced by the body to fight a particular infection; immune - protected against a disease; respiratory - connected with breathing; stagnant - (of water) not flowing; contagious - spreading from one person to another by contact; nausea - a feeling of sickness with an urge to vomit; fatal - causing death; display - to show or exhibit; inflammation - a painful swelling of part of the body; intense - very strong or extreme; pronounced - very noticeable or marked.
explanation: This vocabulary exercise helps learners infer the meaning of difficult words from context and then confirm them from the glossary at the end of the book.

question: Work in pairs and see how many of these words you can use in your own sentences. The pair that will make the most correct sentences will be the winner.
answer: Model sentences: 1. Malaria is caused by a parasite called plasmodium. 2. The disease is transmitted to humans by the bite of an infected mosquito. 3. The virus enters the body through the saliva of the mosquito. 4. In severe cases, the blood may clot inside the vessels. 5. The patient had high fever along with chills. 6. Constipation and kidney dysfunction are seen in some malaria patients. 7. Disorientation may occur when the brain is affected. 8. A blood transfusion can also spread dengue. 9. Our body produces antibodies to fight the infection. 10. A person who has once recovered from chikungunya becomes immune to it. 11. Dengue can cause respiratory difficulties. 12. Mosquitoes breed in stagnant water. 13. Chikungunya is not contagious from person to person. 14. Nausea and vomiting are common in chikungunya. 15. The disease is rarely fatal. 16. The rashes display a clear pattern on the skin. 17. Joint pain and inflammation are severe in chikungunya. 18. The eye pain may become intense with bright light. 19. The joint pain caused by chikungunya is more pronounced than that of dengue. 20. A parasite lives on another living organism.
explanation: This pair-work task gives learners practice in using the new vocabulary of the reading text actively in their own sentences.

answer: d) red blood cells
explanation: The text states that the parasite infects the red blood cells until they burst, so the correct option is (d).
optionsRaw: (a) white blood cells (b) brain (c) stomach (d) red blood cells

answer: a) immune system
explanation: The passage explains that the dengue virus attacks white blood cells and other antibodies, thus affecting the immune system.

answer: b) rashes
explanation: The text states that chikungunya is usually accompanied by fever and skin rash, so option (b) is correct.

question: Read the text and complete the following table in your notebooks: Disease | Source(s) of Transmission | Organs/Cells Attacked | Symptoms.
answer: 1) Malaria - Source(s) of transmission: bite of an infected mosquito (the parasite plasmodium is injected through the mosquito's saliva). Organs/cells attacked: red blood cells (leading to severe liver infection and, if blood flow to the brain stops, cerebral malaria). Symptoms: high fever up to 40 degrees Celsius, chills, sweating, constipation, kidney dysfunction and disorientation. 2) Dengue - Source(s) of transmission: bite of an infected mosquito; also infected blood transfusion, organ donation and from mother to child. Organs/cells attacked: white blood cells and antibodies (the immune system); also the capillaries. Symptoms: high fever, severe body pain, pain behind the eyes that increases with bright light, decreased urine output, respiratory difficulties, intense headache, skin rashes and excessive bleeding from the nose and gums. 3) Chikungunya - Source(s) of transmission: bite of an infected mosquito (which breeds near stagnant or polluted water). Organs/cells attacked: muscle cells, joints, skin, connective tissues and even the central nervous system. Symptoms: fever, skin rash almost identical to dengue rash, headache, nausea, vomiting, muscle weakness, severe joint pain and partial loss of taste.
explanation: The table organises the key information about the three mosquito-borne diseases from the reading passage.

question: What are the most common diseases caused by mosquito bites?
answer: The most common diseases caused by mosquito bites are malaria, dengue and chikungunya. All three are spread by mosquitoes.
explanation: The opening paragraph of the passage states that malaria, dengue and chikungunya are all spread by mosquitoes.

question: Which specific part of the body becomes highly infected in Cerebral Malaria?
answer: In cerebral malaria the brain becomes highly infected. When the infected red blood cells become sticky and clot easily, the flow of blood to the brain stops, causing cerebral malaria.
explanation: The passage links cerebral malaria with the stoppage of blood flow to the brain.

question: What can lead to severe liver infection when one has malaria?
answer: In malaria the parasite infects the red blood cells until they burst. The newly developed plasmodium from the burst red blood cells spreads and infects more red blood cells throughout the body, killing all the cells. This process can lead to severe liver infection.
explanation: The passage explains that the spread of the parasite from burst red blood cells to fresh ones can cause severe liver infection.

question: How is the immune system affected through dengue?
answer: Once the dengue virus enters the body, it circulates around the body and attacks the white blood cells and other antibodies, thus affecting the immune system. The virus then replicates within the cell until the cell bursts and dies. The death of the white blood cells results in leakage of other fluids from the cells, leading to low protein, fluid in the lungs and stomach area, low blood pressure, shock and eventually death.
explanation: The text describes how dengue damages the white blood cells that form an important part of the immune system.

question: How often can one get infected with chikungunya? Why?
answer: One can normally get infected with chikungunya only once in life. The reason is that the virus remains in the system for five to seven days and, once a person recovers from the infection, he or she becomes immune to it for the rest of life.
explanation: The passage states that after recovery from chikungunya a person is immune to it for the rest of their life.

question: Which two of the three diseases have similar symptoms? What are these?
answer: Chikungunya and dengue have almost identical symptoms and disease processes, so much so that one can be mistaken for the other. Both display joint pain and skin rashes that are almost identical. However, the joint pain and inflammation caused by chikungunya are more intense and pronounced, while low platelet count, high bleeding risk and pain behind the eyes are the main symptoms of dengue.
explanation: The passage compares chikungunya and dengue and notes that their symptoms are very similar but with some differences.

question: How often does one have fever and chills when one has malaria?
answer: In malaria the main symptoms are chills or shivering, followed by fever and sweating. These symptoms usually occur every two days.
explanation: The passage states that the fever and chills of malaria typically recur every two days.

question: How do all these diseases affect our life?
answer: All these diseases, that is, malaria, dengue and chikungunya, affect a person's health. They affect the quality of one's work because it takes some time to recover from the weakness caused by them. They also cause loss of working days, weakness, pain and, in severe cases, death, which disturbs the whole family and the community.
explanation: The passage explains that these diseases reduce the quality of a person's work and make recovery slow because of the weakness they cause.

question: How can we protect ourselves from these three diseases?
answer: We can protect ourselves by: wearing clothes that keep us fully covered; using net coverings; living in hygienic surroundings; ensuring that there is no stagnant water, whether clean or dirty, in our locality, not even in uncovered buckets, pots, cans or other things; applying good quality mosquito repellent lotion or natural repellent products; taking extra precaution from dawn to dusk; and seeking medical help as soon as possible.
explanation: The passage gives a list of preventive measures under the heading 'Prevention'.

question: What should we do if we want to recover quickly from these diseases?
answer: If we want to recover quickly from these diseases, we should seek immediate medical help as soon as we observe the symptoms of these diseases. Because the earlier they are treated, the quicker the recovery.
explanation: The closing lines of the passage advise seeking immediate medical help for faster recovery.

question: You have heard on the news about the spread of malaria, dengue and chikungunya in the nearby villages. You and your classmates decide to launch a campaign to create awareness about these diseases. Work in groups of three and develop a flow chart of one disease (malaria / chikungunya / dengue) following the flow chart given (Disease - Cause(s) - Symptoms - Prevention - Advice).
answer: Model flow chart on MALARIA: MALARIA -> CAUSE(S): Caused by plasmodium, a single-celled parasite, often transmitted by infected mosquitoes and injected into a person's circulatory system through the mosquito's saliva. -> SYMPTOMS: High fever up to 40 degrees Celsius, chills and shivering, sweating, constipation, kidney dysfunction and disorientation. -> PREVENTION: Wear clothes that keep you fully covered; use net coverings; live in hygienic surroundings; ensure there is no stagnant water in uncovered buckets, pots or cans; apply mosquito repellent; and take extra precaution from dawn to dusk. -> ADVICE: Seek medical help as soon as you notice the symptoms, because the earlier the disease is treated, the quicker the recovery. (A group working on dengue would use: Cause(s) - four types of dengue viruses spread by mosquito bites, also by infected blood transfusion, organ donation or from mother to child; Symptoms - high fever, severe body pain, pain behind the eyes, decreased urine output, rashes and excessive bleeding from nose and gums; Prevention - the same protective steps as above; Advice - seek immediate medical help. A group working on chikungunya would use: Cause(s) - a virus transmitted by mosquitoes that breed near stagnant or polluted water; Symptoms - fever, skin rash, headache, nausea, vomiting, muscle weakness and severe joint pain; Prevention - the same protective steps; Advice - see a doctor at once and rest well.)
explanation: This group activity asks learners to organise the information about one disease into an awareness flow chart using the pattern Disease, Cause(s), Symptoms, Prevention and Advice.

question: Work in pairs. Practise the dialogue between Shama and Ahmer orally, then add one more dialogue of your own. Complete the missing lines (Ahmer and Shama).
answer: Completed dialogue. Ahmer: Are you satisfied with the way the teacher explained the poem today? Shama: Well, to tell you the truth, I didn't really understand what he explained. I still have a number of things to ask him. What about you? Ahmer: No, I'm dissatisfied. I don't think the teacher was prepared. But yesterday he explained the vocabulary very well. What do you say? Shama: You're right. The class was fun. I loved the way he made us all get up and move around to find the right meanings. Ahmer: I was very satisfied with yesterday's lesson too, but today I was quite disappointed. Shama: Let us ask him politely to explain the poem once again tomorrow. Additional dialogue of our own. Ahmer: I am extremely happy with the way the teacher treats us when we ask questions. Shama: Yes, but I don't like the way the homework is given at the last moment. Ahmer: I agree. I hope tomorrow's explanation will be clearer. Shama: I am sure it will be, and then we will all be satisfied.
explanation: This speaking task gives practice in expressing satisfaction and dissatisfaction politely, using the phrases given in the boxes.

question: Context 1: Sharif and Rayan took a train to Multan. They had reserved seats in the air conditioned compartment. Mostly things were very good and the seats were comfortable. However, when the train started, they found that the air conditioning wasn't working. Role play a dialogue expressing satisfaction with some things and dissatisfaction with the air conditioning.
answer: Model dialogue. Sharif: I am really satisfied with the train service today - the seats are comfortable and the compartment is very clean. Rayan: Yes, I'm extremely happy with the seating and the cleanliness. But I'm very disappointed with the air conditioning, as it is not working at all. Sharif: You're right. I don't like the way the air conditioning has failed on such a hot day. Rayan: Let's call the caretaker and tell him politely about it. Caretaker: Yes, how can I help you? Sharif: We are satisfied with everything else, but the air conditioner in our compartment isn't working. Could you please get it repaired? Caretaker: I'm sorry for the inconvenience. I will get it checked right away. Rayan: Thank you. We are very happy with your prompt response.
explanation: The role play requires the learners to express both satisfaction and dissatisfaction politely using the given phrases.

question: Context 2: The power supply system in your area is generally good, and complaints are usually solved promptly. However, there has been a power breakdown for 48 hours that has not been solved in spite of repeated complaints. You and a group of neighbours go to the electricity department to complain. Role play a dialogue expressing general satisfaction and current dissatisfaction.
answer: Model dialogue. Spokesman: Good morning. We are satisfied with the electricity service in our area in general, because complaints are usually solved in a timely manner. Officer: Thank you very much for that. What is the problem now? Spokesman: We are very dissatisfied at the moment. There has been a power breakdown in our neighbourhood for 48 hours, and the problem has not been solved in spite of our repeated complaints. Officer: I am sorry for the inconvenience. There is a fault in the main cable, and our team is working on it. Spokesman: We are disappointed with the delay, as it has caused great hardship to the whole street, especially to students and old people. Officer: I understand your concern. The supply should be restored within a few hours. Spokesman: Thank you. We are happy with the good service generally, and we hope the fault will be fixed soon.
explanation: This context trains learners to balance general satisfaction with current dissatisfaction in a polite complaint.

question: Context 3: You are a teacher in a school. Your student Khalid usually does very well in all the tests, but in the last couple of tests his performance has been unsatisfactory. Call him and express your satisfaction with his work generally and dissatisfaction with the way he has been performing lately. Ask him how he feels about his own progress.
answer: Model dialogue. Teacher: Khalid, I called you to talk about your work. I have always been very satisfied with your performance, as you usually do very well in all the tests. Khalid: Thank you, sir. Teacher: However, I am not happy with the way you have been performing in the last couple of tests. Your marks have dropped, and I am quite disappointed with this sudden change. Khalid: I am sorry, sir. I have not been keeping well, and I could not revise properly. Teacher: I understand, but you must not let your studies suffer. How do you feel about your own progress? Khalid: I am not satisfied with my progress either, sir. I have promised myself to work harder and get back to my usual standard. Teacher: I am glad to hear that. I hope you will improve in the coming tests.
explanation: The role play practises polite expression of satisfaction and dissatisfaction in a teacher-student conversation.

question: Look at the sentences in the table. Against each sentence put a tick in the column that identifies whether it is a simple or a compound sentence. Sentence 1: This year has started on a positive note for the students.
answer: Simple sentence. (It has one subject and one predicate.)
explanation: The book gives this sentence as the example; it contains a single subject 'This year' and a single predicate, so it is simple.

question: The classrooms smell of fresh paint, as they were painted during the holidays.
answer: Compound sentence. ('The classrooms smell of fresh paint' and 'they were painted during the holidays' are two complete sentences joined by comma + 'as'.)
explanation: It contains two independent clauses joined by the conjunction 'as' with a comma, so it is compound.

question: The students love the newly painted classrooms, and they like the newly polished desks.
answer: Compound sentence. (Two complete sentences joined by comma + 'and'.)
explanation: Two independent clauses are joined by comma + 'and', making it a compound sentence.

question: Their motivation has increased and their enthusiasm is clearly visible.
answer: Compound sentence. (Two complete sentences joined by 'and'.)
explanation: It has two independent clauses joined by the coordinating conjunction 'and', so it is compound.

question: Most of the students come to school regularly now.
answer: Simple sentence. (One subject and one predicate.)
explanation: The sentence has a single subject 'Most of the students' and a single predicate, so it is simple.

question: They actively participate in various class activities.
answer: Simple sentence. (One subject and one predicate.)
explanation: It contains only one independent clause, so it is simple.

question: The students enjoy being outdoors, because they all like sports activities.
answer: Compound sentence. (Two complete sentences joined by comma + 'because'.)
explanation: Two independent clauses are joined by comma + 'because', so it is compound.

question: They are happy with the new look of the school, but they are not happy with the sports facilities that they have.
answer: Compound sentence. (Two complete sentences joined by comma + 'but'.)
explanation: Two independent clauses are joined by comma + 'but', so it is compound.

question: They have requested their principal for better sports and game facilities.
answer: Simple sentence. (One subject and one predicate.)
explanation: It has a single subject and a single predicate, so it is simple.

question: The students are hopeful that they will have good facilities soon, because their principal has promised that new play grounds will be developed.
answer: Compound sentence. (Two complete sentences joined by comma + 'because'.)
explanation: Two independent clauses are joined by comma + 'because', so it is compound.

question: Join the two sentences to form a compound sentence, using any conjunction: Najma and Rehana studied very hard. They both got A grades in their exams.
answer: Najma and Rehana studied very hard, so they both got A grades in their exams.
explanation: The conjunction 'so' shows the result of studying hard, joining the two clauses into a compound sentence.

question: Her father is a pilot. He has flown many different types of planes.
answer: Her father is a pilot, and he has flown many different types of planes.
explanation: The conjunction 'and' adds a related piece of information, joining the two clauses into a compound sentence.

question: Our car is very old. Its engine is in good condition.
answer: Our car is very old, but its engine is in good condition.
explanation: The conjunction 'but' shows contrast between the age of the car and the good condition of its engine.

question: The boys were playing cricket. It was the first day of their summer vacations.
answer: The boys were playing cricket, for it was the first day of their summer vacations.
explanation: The conjunction 'for' or 'because' gives the reason, joining the two clauses into a compound sentence.

question: My brother is a good artist. He cannot sing at all.
answer: My brother is a good artist, but he cannot sing at all.
explanation: The conjunction 'but' shows the contrast between his skill as an artist and his inability to sing.

question: You may buy only a new dress now. You may buy a new dress and new shoes next month.
answer: You may buy only a new dress now, or you may buy a new dress and new shoes next month.
explanation: The conjunction 'or' presents a choice between two alternatives, joining the clauses into a compound sentence.

question: The baby cannot walk. The baby can crawl very fast.
answer: The baby cannot walk, but the baby can crawl very fast.
explanation: The conjunction 'but' contrasts the baby's inability to walk with the ability to crawl fast.

question: I love gardening. I can grow my own fresh vegetables.
answer: I love gardening, for I can grow my own fresh vegetables.
explanation: The conjunction 'for' or 'because' gives the reason, joining the two clauses into a compound sentence.

question: The flowers in this pot are very colourful. The flowers in your garden have a lovely fragrance.
answer: The flowers in this pot are very colourful, and the flowers in your garden have a lovely fragrance.
explanation: The conjunction 'and' joins two related statements about the flowers into a compound sentence.

question: This book is very informative. It is also very interesting.
answer: This book is very informative, and it is also very interesting.
explanation: The conjunction 'and' adds a second quality of the book, joining the clauses into a compound sentence.

question: Work in pairs and write sentences in your notebooks by following the steps: Step 1 - Write 8-10 simple sentences about the people and things in your classroom. Step 2 - Write one more simple sentence for each of the sentences you have written. Step 3 - Join the simple sentences to form compound sentences.
answer: Step 1 (simple sentences): 1. Our classroom is very big. 2. Samir is reading a book. 3. Ayesha is writing on the whiteboard. 4. The teacher is explaining the lesson. 5. There are thirty students in our class. 6. The walls are painted light blue. 7. There are two fans in the room. 8. Ali is sharpening his pencil. 9. The windows are open. 10. Sana is smiling at her friend. Step 2 (one more simple sentence for each): 1. Our classroom is very big. It does not have enough light. 2. Samir is reading a book. He seems to be enjoying it. 3. Ayesha is writing on the whiteboard. Her handwriting is very neat. 4. The teacher is explaining the lesson. The students are listening carefully. 5. There are thirty students in our class. They come from different areas. 6. The walls are painted light blue. The paint looks fresh. 7. There are two fans in the room. Both of them are working well. 8. Ali is sharpening his pencil. He is making too much noise. 9. The windows are open. Fresh air is coming in. 10. Sana is smiling at her friend. She looks very happy. Step 3 (compound sentences): 1. Our classroom is very big, but it does not have enough light. 2. Samir is reading a book, and he seems to be enjoying it. 3. Ayesha is writing on the whiteboard, and her handwriting is very neat. 4. The teacher is explaining the lesson, and the students are listening carefully. 5. There are thirty students in our class, and they come from different areas. 6. The walls are painted light blue, and the paint looks fresh. 7. There are two fans in the room, and both of them are working well. 8. Ali is sharpening his pencil, but he is making too much noise. 9. The windows are open, so fresh air is coming in. 10. Sana is smiling at her friend, for she looks very happy.
explanation: This guided writing task moves learners from simple sentences to compound sentences through three clear steps, as shown in the book's model.

question: Sabiha keeps repeating the same words in her letter to her friend Munira. Help her write a mix of simple and compound sentences to make her writing interesting. Rewrite the letter (Sabiha's letter to Munira, pages 120-121).
answer: Sabiha's letter to Munira. I have some exciting news for you about my town, for there is a 'Housing boom' in our town. Builders are building new houses, and they are planning to build at least 300 new houses. These houses are small, so they can easily accommodate single families. The houses will be mainly two storeyed. The people of our town are really excited, and they think that the town needs new people and new business. It will be nice to have new people and new friends. More people will mean more progress for our town, but more people will also require more facilities. New roads will have to be built, and more transport facilities will be required. We will have to build more schools, and we will also need to build more colleges. The town will need more shopping areas, and it will also have to provide other facilities. New water and electricity facilities will have to be provided. Some people are not so happy, for they feel that more people will make the town crowded. There will be more electricity problems and more pollution. There will be more garbage in the town, and there will be more vehicles and factories. Travelling in the town will take a longer time, because there will be more traffic. The houses will be built soon, and they are expected to be built within two years. Many people are interested, for many people want to buy a house in our town. The town is being connected to the port through a new highway. The town is near a river, so water can be supplied easily to the town from the river. Many people have already selected their property, but there are still properties available. Those interested in buying a house should hurry, for all the houses will soon be sold. People can contact the builders, and the builder's office can give them more details.
explanation: The rewritten letter mixes simple and compound sentences, and uses suitable conjunctions (and, but, so, for, because) to avoid the repetition of short sentences in the original.

question: Change from direct to indirect speech: "I have many friends and I have to invite all of them tomorrow," said Abid.
answer: Abid said that he had many friends and he had to invite all of them the next day.
explanation: A statement is changed with 'said that'; the present tense becomes past ('have' becomes 'had', 'have to' becomes 'had to') and 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'.

question: Change from direct to indirect speech: Reshma said, "I hope I will get admission in the medical college this year."
answer: Reshma hoped that she would get admission in the medical college that year.
explanation: 'Said + hope' becomes 'hoped'; 'will' becomes 'would' and 'this year' becomes 'that year'.

question: Change from direct to indirect speech: "I wish I had ten hands and a hundred fingers to do all this work," said Feroza.
answer: Feroza wished that she had ten hands and a hundred fingers to do all that work.
explanation: 'Said + wish' becomes 'wished'; 'this' becomes 'that'. The past subjunctive 'had' does not change.

question: Change from direct to indirect speech: The student said, "I promise I will do my homework regularly from today."
answer: The student promised that he would do his homework regularly from that day.
explanation: 'Said + promise' becomes 'promised'; 'will' becomes 'would' and 'today' becomes 'that day'.

question: Change from direct to indirect speech: "They want to buy a new car," said the lawyer, "but they don't have any money."
answer: The lawyer said that they wanted to buy a new car but they did not have any money.
explanation: 'Said that' is used, the present tense becomes past ('want' becomes 'wanted', 'don't have' becomes 'did not have'), and the two parts of the quotation are joined into one statement.

question: Change from direct to indirect speech: "We hope we will be able to get permission from our parents," said the children.
answer: The children hoped that they would be able to get permission from their parents.
explanation: 'Said + hope' becomes 'hoped'; 'we' becomes 'they', 'our' becomes 'their', and 'will' becomes 'would'.

question: Change from direct to indirect speech: "I never thought that a son of mine would get such bad marks!" said his father.
answer: His father exclaimed that he had never thought that a son of his would get such bad marks.
explanation: The exclamation is changed with 'exclaimed that'; the past tense 'thought' becomes 'had thought' and 'mine' becomes 'his'.

question: Change from direct to indirect speech: The blind boy said, "I wish I could see this interesting match on the television."
answer: The blind boy wished that he could see that interesting match on the television.
explanation: 'Said + wish' becomes 'wished'; 'this' becomes 'that'. The modal 'could' remains unchanged.

question: Change from direct to indirect speech: "Next week, we promise, we will clean the whole house," the children said to their parents.
answer: The children promised their parents that the following week they would clean the whole house.
explanation: 'Said + promise' becomes 'promised'; 'next week' becomes 'the following week' and 'will' becomes 'would'.

question: Change from direct to indirect speech: "Our team has won the champion's trophy here for the first time!" said the coach.
answer: The coach exclaimed that their team had won the champion's trophy there for the first time.
explanation: The exclamation is changed with 'exclaimed that'; the present perfect 'has won' becomes past perfect 'had won' and 'here' becomes 'there'.

question: Work in pairs, read the story 'Avoiding Criticism' and put all the direct speech sentences into indirect speech. The story has statements, exclamations, wishes, promises and hopes.
answer: Avoiding Criticism. Nasrudin and his son were travelling with their donkey. Nasrudin preferred to walk while his son rode the donkey. Soon they passed a group of bystanders, and one of them said that the boy was so selfish, adding that he was riding on a donkey while his poor old father was forced to walk alongside. Another man said that it was so disrespectful and exclaimed what a horrible and spoiled child he was. Nasrudin and his son felt embarrassed, so they changed places - this time Nasrudin rode the donkey while his son walked. Nasrudin said to himself that he hoped he was doing the right thing then. Soon they passed another group of people. Seeing them, one of them exclaimed that the poor young boy had to walk while his selfish father was riding the donkey, and added that he was a heartless parent. Nasrudin was upset to hear this. He said that he wished people would mind their own business. Since he wanted to avoid any further comments, he decided that both he and his son would ride the donkey at the same time. As they both rode, they passed another group of people. One bystander commented that that man and his son were so cruel, adding that they were forcing that poor donkey to bear the weight of two people and that they should be put in jail for that act. Nasrudin heard this and told his son that the only way they could avoid people's comments was that they both walked. The son replied that he supposed that his father was right. Nasrudin said happily that he promised that nobody would be able to say anything to them as they were doing the right thing that time. So they got off the donkey and continued on foot. But as they passed another group of people, they heard them laughing. They said that those people were so stupid that both of them were walking in that heat and neither of them was riding the donkey, and exclaimed what foolish people they were.
explanation: All the direct speech in the story is converted to indirect speech following the rules for statements, exclamations, wishes, promises and hopes (tenses shifted back, pronouns and time/place words changed).

question: Work in pairs and write a descriptive essay of at least four paragraphs on one of the following topics: 1. My favourite Aunt / Uncle  2. A teacher that I remember  3. Our school principal  4. My grandmother / grandfather.
answer: A Teacher That I Remember. Of all the teachers I have met, the one I remember most fondly is Miss Saima, who taught us English in class seven. She was not just a teacher; she was a friend, a guide and an inspiration to the whole class. Even today, whenever I think of my early school days, her smiling face comes to my mind at once. Miss Saima was a slim and graceful lady of about forty. She always dressed neatly in simple, light-coloured shalwar kameez with a matching dupatta. Her hair was tied back in a tidy bun, and she wore thin, round spectacles that made her look wise and kind. Her most striking feature was her warm smile, which could put even the shyest student at ease. She spoke in a soft, clear voice that was a pleasure to listen to, and her bright eyes always sparkled with interest and affection. What made Miss Saima truly memorable, however, was her patience and her love for teaching. She would explain a difficult lesson again and again until every single student understood it. If any of us made a mistake, she never scolded us harshly; instead, she would gently point out the error and encourage us to try again. She was particularly fond of reading, and she taught us to love books by telling us wonderful stories after every lesson. Her cheerful nature and her sense of humour turned even the dullest grammar lesson into an enjoyable experience. Miss Saima left our school many years ago, but her influence on me has never faded. She was the person who first taught me to love the English language, and it is because of her that I still enjoy reading and writing today. She was hard-working, kind, patient and full of warmth, and these are the qualities that make her the teacher I will always remember.
explanation: The essay describes a person in four paragraphs - introduction, appearance, qualities and behaviour, and why the person is memorable - as required by the descriptive essay guidelines.

question: Work in pairs and ask each other the following questions. One student plays Student A and the other Student B. Read the dialogue and fill in the blanks given below. Student A: You look quite stressed, what's the problem? Student B: The problem is that we are short of money and I can't pay my fees. Student A: Since when have you been worried? Student B: Ever since my father told me that .... Student A: Have you talked to anybody about this? Student B: No, I don't know .... Student B: Who do you think I should talk to? Student A: Well, you could talk to .... Maybe, someone can help. Student B: What should I do in the meantime? Student A: You should .... Student B: Do you think I will be able to arrange something? Student A: I'm sure ....
answer: Completed dialogue. Student A: You look quite stressed, what's the problem? Student B: The problem is that we are short of money and I can't pay my fees. Student A: Since when have you been worried? Student B: Ever since my father told me that he had lost his job and that our income had suddenly stopped. Student A: Have you talked to anybody about this? Student B: No, I don't know whom I should talk to about such a personal problem. Student B: Who do you think I should talk to? Student A: Well, you could talk to our class teacher. Maybe, someone can help. Student B: What should I do in the meantime? Student A: You should explain your situation to the principal and request him to give you some time to pay the fees. Student B: Do you think I will be able to arrange something? Student A: I'm sure you will find a way out, and I will help you in whatever way I can.
explanation: This listening-and-speaking task practises informal interviewing, reciprocal language and appropriate responses while discussing a friend's personal problem.

question: Work in pairs and select one of the following situations for an informal interview, or think of another situation: (i) Your friend has severe fever (ii) Cleanliness of toilets in schools (iii) Your brother wants to buy a mobile phone. Discuss how you will deal with the situation, prepare three to four questions, informally interview each other, prepare notes and report to the class.
answer: Model informal interview on Situation (i) 'Your friend has severe fever'. Preparation questions asked by the interviewer: 1. Since when have you had this high fever? 2. Have you seen a doctor or taken any medicine? 3. What symptoms, such as headache, body ache or shivering, do you have? 4. Have you told your parents about it? Responses received (notes): Fever started two days ago; temperature is very high and comes with shivering; has taken only a paracetamol tablet so far; has not seen a doctor yet; parents have been informed. Report to the class: My friend has been suffering from severe fever for the last two days, with shivering and body ache. He has taken only a paracetamol tablet and has not yet consulted a doctor. I have advised him to drink plenty of water, take complete rest, and visit a doctor immediately so that the illness is properly treated and does not become serious. (For Situation (ii) 'Cleanliness of toilets in schools' the questions would be: How often are the school toilets cleaned? Is clean water and soap available there? What problems do students face? What can be done to improve them? For Situation (iii) the questions would be: Why do you want a mobile phone? How much can you spend? Have you discussed it with our parents? How will you use it responsibly?)
explanation: This task develops interviewing skills - preparing relevant questions, listening attentively, taking notes and reporting the findings to the class, as described in the tip boxes on page 127.

question: Vocabulary building - Word chain: In groups of four, write a new word beginning with the last alphabet of the previous word. You cannot repeat words, and each word must have a minimum of four letters. The book's example is: chain - number - ring - grow - elephant - think. Create your own word chain.
answer: Model word chain (each word begins with the last letter of the previous word, has at least four letters, and is used only once): house -> engine -> eggs -> snail -> lemon -> nest -> table -> eight -> tree -> energy -> yard -> dark -> kite -> artist -> star -> rain -> night -> tower -> river -> round. A shorter sample that matches the book's example: chain -> number -> ring -> grow -> wide -> elephant -> tree -> early -> yard -> desk.
explanation: This fun vocabulary activity helps learners revise spelling and vocabulary by forming a chain in which every new word starts with the last letter of the previous word.
